text: There’s an interesting pricing issue where the all-in cost of something is often much more than the nominal cost of it, and so the nominal thing could actually be priced much higher, because the demand is so inelastic. For example. Say I pay $10 to go to an event, but I pay $20 for an Uber there, and $20 for an Uber back. My all-in cost is $50. They could’ve made the event 50% or 100% more expensive and it would’ve barely moved the needle. I would’ve easily paid.
author: @johnloeber

text: one of the most interesting, intricately precise descriptions of self-deception I’ve ever read is by a magician talking about his late realization that he was overweight. he “knew” all his life he was fat, and yet it still came as a shock to him when he developed medical troubles
author: Visakan Veerasamy

text: On a somewhat related note, small / big probability events are likely to be significantly mispriced when they are long-dated due to the opportunity cost of capital, as traders discount the value of tying up money in a low/high-probability outcome instead of deploying it in higher-yielding investments, i.e. market participants require additional compensation for illiquidity and opportunity cost as well as risk.
author: Lihon

text: Intellectual to intellectual: Stop watching endless documentaries. Stop dissecting podcasts. Stop scrolling through think pieces and “10 ways to fix your mind” threads. Start reading fiction. Start watching cartoons and comfort shows. Go outside without headphones. Let your brain breathe. Constant self-improvement isn’t evolution, it’s brain rot disguised as productivity. You don’t need to study every emotion to heal it. Not everything that hurts needs to be analyzed. Some things just need to be lived through. You don’t need to turn every feeling into a theory. Sometimes peace is found in doing something that doesn’t need to make sense. You’re not here just to understand life. You’re here to feel it.
author: @WarpaintJournal

text: Spiritual lesson I’ve learned over the years: you have to include yourself in the money. . . . This whole life thing really isn’t that serious – and when you take a step back and get your inner stuff in alignment, things can line up faster than you’d ever imagine. One day you wake up and it all clicks. Today might have been that day.

The high ratio of design space to practitioners in fine art has combined with the practical importance of attribution to give people the impression that painting in a distinctively Leonardesque way is what makes Leonardo good.
author: Paul Graham

text: The guy who does better than you probably views the game the opposite way. He actually wants the ball. He smiles like a psycho when he’s on an island with the best defender. He gets excited when that girl walks in. You’re just nervous. . . . Not something you can change over night but push yourself a little. Stop hiding when the game isn’t even important. Take the big shot and miss a couple times. It’s the idiot who can’t shoot who banks the game-winner half the time anyway
author: @sidewalkthougt

text: To valorize agency without also emphasizing its purpose allows us to ignore harder questions like: How do I live a good life? And what about the collective good? The smash-and-grab mentality elides these questions. Have we forgotten that life might be better lived in concert with others?
author: Sophie Haigney

text: But it struck me that in a different time, we would have called that “courage.” That word has fallen out of fashion. And there’s a reason. “Courage” has a moral valence that agency doesn’t. Agency is about action, but it tells us nothing of direction.
author: Sophie Haigney

text: Self-optimising is desperate because this level of narcissistic self-absorption makes people oblivious to society at large. Profound and systemic issues like the housing crisis . . . are all buried under daily affirmations about acceptance and calmness.
author: Jacob Phillips

text: We’re so focused on becoming acceptable that we’ve forgotten we might already be accepted — if we’d just show up as ourselves and let people in.
author: Hanna Horvath

text: What I AM saying is: notice. Notice when “self-improvement” is actually “performance for others.” Notice when the definition of “optimal” isn’t yours — when it’s been handed to you by an algorithm or an industry or a culture that profits from your dissatisfaction. Notice when every step of “bettering yourself” requires a purchase. Notice when optimizing is isolating you from the people who would accept you as you are. The gamification of selfhood has a way of making life feel like a series of levels to beat rather than something to actually live. We’re so busy optimizing that we forget to ask what we’re optimizing for — and whether the answer is actually ours.
author: Hanna Horvath

text: just saw a girl explain that she tried to get rejected 1000 times in 2025 and ended up being cast in plays, winning beauty pageants, securing paid brand deals, appearing in commercials. this is your sign to chase rejection to the point of “accidental” success. you’ll be surprised.
author: ask a girl Substack

text: Happy chaos is better than structured routines
author: Danielle Franz

text: But the whole notion of having to defend literature or the humanities in the first place may have us wrong-footed. It’s not only what you learn from reading Moby-Dick—notwithstanding Melville’s extensive knowledge of 19th-century whaling—but what you are doing when you are reading Moby-Dick. You are neither learning a transferable skill nor escaping from the world’s demands that you do. You are not word-maxxing or optimizing information for efficiency. You are engaged in a singular practice, one with its own primary justification.
author: Walt Hunter

text: one day you will look back and wonder why you even worried
I just think it’s neat that Shakespeare decided to cap off his career in the theatre by writing the only honest poems ever written
author: @molochofficial

text: Here’s the real secret, no amount of pomodoros or productivity hacks will restore the deep focus you are craving. It’s a flow state that can only be accessed by putting your mind truly at rest. You know what’s not restful? Rapid-fire stimulation, ad clutter, and live-streamed war crimes next to photos of your baby nephew next to branded partnerships for an LED face mask.
author: Katie Lowe

text: Yet my goal isn’t even to “win” a battle against these people, it is more about participating in a long tradition of engaging with an intellectual commons in a positive-sum way. More simply, my own goals are to stay connected to myself, have the energy and excitement to stay on this journey, and be inspired to continue to create.
author: Paul Millerd

text: That’s where we enter the realm of perspectival knowing: Agency as a way of looking. Your worldview determines your affordances, the “handles” reality offers you. For example, nothing seems worth doing to a depressed person, while a manic person urgently wants to do everything all at once.
author: Octopusyarn

text: Now people barely bring it up at all. It’s like a lion has escaped the zoo and it’s gulping down schoolchildren, but when people suggest zoo improvements, all the agenda items are like, “We should add another Dippin’ Dots kiosk”. If you bring up the loose tiger, everyone gets annoyed at you, like “Of course, no one likes the tiger”.
author: Adam Mastroianni

text: Every other person be like “I’m such a sensitive and special and secretly tender person with a uniquely hard life, that I needed to become evil and manipulative and battle-hardened to survive”. You’re not that special bro. This is the whisper of the devil and everyone hears it when times get tough. Love and softness will always, always be the ultimate rebellion. But old habits die hard, and here you are pretending we live in a famine/battlefield to simultaneously self-aggrandize while self-pitying while also justifying your low empathy and nonexistent integrity. This is why people are so desperate to find, to create, a battle or an apocalypse, an excuse to never look within. Permission to regress to a dog-eat-dog world. If given peace, many would not know what to do with it.
author: @seashell_luvr

text: She’s right about this and it’s worst for new artists. Many fear the sketchbook because they feel compelled to share everything. Sketches need the right to fail. And that steady flame of internal motive is cultivated from a spark through the mess of exploration.
author: @jholtillus

text: Doing your best means not just doing your best in each moment, but also doing your best to put yourself in a position where it’s easier to make the best choices. Every move that a chess player makes functions to get the board in a state where good plays emerge. Athletes do the same thing – “skate to where the puck is going to be” type of stuff. But few people realize that this is a general strategy to apply in daily life.
author: Justin Skycak

text: That joining a stable company guarantees a stable job. It’s counterintuitive but vital to understand that if you join a stable company, then your job security is actually pretty low, because your leverage is low. The highest job security is when you join an unstable company and . . .
author: Justin Skycak

text: She was fundamentally a broken person, a fantasist. She’d seen the images of wealth and glamour in magazines and fashion blogs, and constructed a delusion in which this, and not the dull, anonymous, small-town existence she’d actually been born into, was her life. For a while, at least, it worked. Her mad dreams slotted perfectly into reality like a key in a lock. Most people are condemned to trudge along in the furrow that the world has dug for them, but a few deranged dreamers really can wish themselves into whatever life they want.
author: Sam Kriss

text: It’s terrifying to ask someone out. What you want is to have the dating site that tells you that algorithmically you’ve been matched with this person, and then magically you have permission to talk to them. I think there’s something similar going on here with AI. Many of these people are smart enough that they could answer their own questions, but they want someone else to do it, because then they don’t have to have this terrifying encounter with their own humanity.
author: “Alexander” (via Harper’s)

text: Black-and-white movies present the deliberate absence of color. This makes them less realistic than color films (for the real world is in color). They are more dreamlike, more pure, composed of shapes and forms and movements and light and shadow. Color films can simply be illuminated. Black-and-white films have to be lighted . . . Black and white is a legitimate and beautiful artistic choice in motion pictures, creating feelings and effects that cannot be obtained any other way.
author: Roger Ebert

text: Idea: “Leisure Fellowship” – find competent socialites under 25 y/o and give them $200,000 to read, write, tinker, workout, host social gatherings and, most importantly, meet people online. My bet is that those people would become both fascinating and well-connected.
author: @PabloPeniche

text: some people internalize a dominance hierarchy where receiving help = act of submission. they only begrudgingly submit to people they acknowledge as their superiors. they refuse to accept help from anybody they perceive as inferior. failing to be helped by therapists serves this
author: Visakan Veerasamy

text: We talk about time as if it’s a straight line, something you spend, save, waste, optimise. But most days, time feels more like weather. It thickens. It thins. It pauses without asking permission. . . . Nothing in a river is in a hurry. Nothing in a tree is trying to “get ahead”. . . . Maybe that’s why certain moments stay with us longer than others. Not because they were important, but because we didn’t interrupt them. . . . Some days don’t need to be productive. Some thoughts don’t need conclusions. Some moments don’t need witnesses. They just need time.
author: Marco Secchi

text: The heartbreak teaches you how to hold joy when it comes back around. The rejection shows you what you actually want. The loneliness is what makes you recognize home when you finally find it. None of it is wasted if you let it change you. The timer is running whether you’re paying attention or not. The fruit is ripening. The light is shifting. Your one wild, temporary life is happening right now, and the only tragedy is treating it like a dress rehearsal. Reach. Risk. Let yourself want things out loud. The worst that happens is you feel everything. The disappointment, the ecstasy, the full spectrum of being alive in a body that won’t last forever. The impermanence isn’t the problem. The impermanence is the point.
author: Vidya Sethi

text: just improvised a talk to a bunch of creatives titled ‘enduring the discomfort of publishing’: stick around for the long haul. a lot of the great rewards (eg people telling you how their work changed their life) take years to pay off. find ways to enjoy the process that aren’t conditional on attention metrics (likes/views/shares). the early years of the process tend to be unrewarding in the conventional sense. it helps to find something that sustains you despite it. you get to encourage the segments of your audience that you want. focus on what you want to see more of. over time this will shape the vibe of your work, your reputation, how people interpret and see you, which in turn affects what people send your way. rapid success is not as desirable as people think; it’ll be overwhelming and disorienting in a bad way. it’s often better to grow at a steady pace such that you [avoid] unpleasant shocks to your system.
author: Visakan Veerasamy

text: It’s only after we’ve lost everything that we’re free to do anything.
author: Tyler Durden, Fight Club

text: You are not playing the same game as everyone else. Their status symbols mean nothing. Their opinions are regurgitated. Their ambitions stem from fear. None of this will work for you, only you can find the right Meta for your life. Stop trying to be perfect. Discipline is overrated when it puts you in a cage.
Stop worrying about what will happen in the future and believe you will be able to figure it out along the way.
I was waiting for something extraordinary to happen, but as the years wasted on, nothing ever did unless I caused it.
author: Charles Bukowski

text: There are players for whom goal and purpose are identical. They pursue what Nguyen calls “achievement play”: professional athletes, for example, play games to win, and believe deeply in the glory of victory. But most of us pursue “striving play,” in which “you try to win not because winning is important, but because the act of trying to win gives you a delicious struggle.” This involves an interior balancing act.
author: Joshua Rothman (on C. Thi Nguyen)

text: In the real world, as in the game world, scores are motivating and clarifying; they can help groups of people coalesce around shared goals. But real-world scores, like game scores, are also reductive.
author: Joshua Rothman (on C. Thi Nguyen)

text: Socialmaxxing. Network is net worth. Not cringe LinkedIn way. Real friends. Deep conversations. People who push you. Family you spend time with. Loneliness epidemic is real. Men isolated. Stuck in bedrooms optimising morning routines while relationships fall apart. No amount of self-improvement replaces people you love. BBQs. Dinners. Trips. Time together. That’s what life’s about.

If every time someone asks you a question, you try to say the right answer . . . your entire life is a test. And when did you have the most anxiety? On Test day. I’m not trying to do the right thing – I am just doing what I FEEL is right.
author: Kanye West

text: Ignore financial nihilism. Cynicism and nihilism were cool in high school, and they sound smart on Substack and Twitter. But they lead you nowhere. This doesn’t mean you should never be bearish. It just means that no amount of wishing we were still in the 1990s or 1950s will bring us back there. Successful traders are open-minded and forward-looking.
author: Brent Donnelly

text: Cal Newport basically solved for this in So Good They Can’t Ignore You. You need the combination of competency, autonomy, and growth to not get burnt out. In simpler terms, you need: Upside; To be good at the thing (or have the capacity to be good); And you need to feel like you have control
author: @TJ_Bongiorno

text: Interesting thought – perhaps video games have just absolutely perfected the flow zone through live player feedback data
author: @benny_equity

I think that creates the interesting question of what actually causes burnout. My sense is it’s often a feeling of a lack of progress, or a lack of a reward, or a missing sense of purpose, potentially not enough dopamine, and maybe social norms.
author: @maxmarchione

text: I saw my life branching out before me like the green fig tree in the story.
author: Sylvia Plath

text: Of course, it is especially important when dealing with others. Kindness and attentiveness exist when you decide. It is thinking about the other person before yourself. You can lay the groundwork to work from, which makes their life easier. You reduce their mental effort and don’t place all the computation on them.

text: With my two boys, I do my best to illustrate the differences between the feverish, relentless dopa hits they get from TikTok and Instagram versus the slower, incremental results that are more valuable and satisfying from reading, working out, or spending time outside – slow dopa, or “Slowpa,” as I call it. . . . Dinner, but also Slowpa.
author: Scott Galloway

text: Children today are overprotected in the real world and under-protected online – an observation made by my NYU colleague Jonathan Haidt.
author: Scott Galloway

text: Success comes when you put in small, consistent amounts of effort, every day and every week; it doesn’t matter whether you’re investing, filming two minutes of video content, or lifting dumbbells. Small, deliberate, regular efforts accumulate and in time pay off. In other words, the most powerful force in the universe – Einstein knew this – is compound interest. Aka, Slowpa.
author: Scott Galloway

text: It allows me to expand on things I need to hear. Like when my sister yelled at me for always being indecisive during our run in Topanga Canyon. “I am cool with whatever” wasn’t as chill and relaxed as I thought. I, and the world, have a decisiveness issue. I could waste my entire life overthinking, being indecisive and she let me know that.

text: But there was an awful magnetism about this business.

text: May you be spared the version of me that needed you to keep being exactly who you were.
author: The Shadowed Archive

text: Enemies of Friendship. Self-optimization. Professional networking. Status anxiety disguised as taste. The algorithm’s sweet narcotic drip that replaces “we” with “for you.” . . . Friendship is not spa water. It is the puddle you step in together and then name.
author: The Shadowed Archive

text: Be happy while you are living for you are a long time dead.

text: People see bad things in the world and ask why God doesn’t do something about it. But God did do something. He sent you.

text: The sun still rises on mornings that feel uninhabitable. The bills still come due. . . . There is no great cosmic stillness reserved for your private sorrows. There is only this: life, humming and pulsing and surging forward, as thoughtlessly as blood through a body that does not know how to stop beating.
author: Joy in Abundance Substack

text: working on mediocre things is a disrespect to life. being risk averse is a disrespect to life. waking up and doing things that are not your life’s work is a disrespect to life. not taking a swing at pursuing the biggest opportunity in front of your eyes is a disrespect to life
author: @overac111ever

text: One example of a desirable difficulty involves what is known as the “generation effect.” Simply: forcing yourself to come up with an answer to something before having one given to you primes your brain for subsequent learning. . . . It would seem that, for these essay-writers, ChatGPT was the precise opposite of a desirable difficulty. It allowed the essay writers to give answers before doing their own thinking. Let’s call it an “undesirable ease.”
author: David Epstein

text: The authors of the study argue that early, heavy reliance on the AI seemed to have encouraged “shallow encoding”: The work got done, but it didn’t get deeply integrated into memory. They also use the term “cognitive debt”: If you repeatedly lean on ChatGPT upfront, you defer effort now but pay later, with weaker critical thinking, poorer recall, and more superficial engagement with ideas.
author: David Epstein

text: Testing: Test people before they have a chance to study. It primes your brain and exploits the “hypercorrection” effect. Interleaving: Mixing types of problems will extend the time it takes to learn one type, but improves the broader ability to match the approach to the type. “Difficulty isn’t a sign that you’re not learning but ease is.” Spacing: To maximize stickiness, you actually want to re-learn something just after you have forgotten it!
author: David Epstein (via Kris Abdelmessih)

text: But for me, the best days and moments of my life are not when I am on social media, eat a bunch of junk food, or optimize my day for comfort . . . The days I look back fondly are those when I threw my heart into something and tried to answer the questions life threw at me, no matter if I failed. . . . Moments when I tried to fulfill the expectations of life because life never stops expecting things of me. . . . But if you take a risk and fail, so be it! Never do I regret failing, I regret sitting on social media or plugging in my headphones to avoid something. I never regret living in the real world. I regret living online.
author: Scantron

text: The human beauty we’re talking about here is beauty of a particular type; it might be called kinetic beauty. Its power and appeal are universal. . . . What it seems to have to do with, really, is human beings’ reconciliation with the fact of having a body.
author: David Foster Wallace

text: Because of decreasing application friction, any given opportunity requires more effort to achieve than in earlier generations. Although this can’t lower the average society-wide success level . . . , it can inflict substantial deadweight loss on contenders and a subjective sense of underachievement.
author: Scott Alexander

text: This renewed fascination with embodiment isn’t spontaneous, it’s a reaction to technologies so powerful and frictionless they’re impossible to ignore. Even the most grounded among us now move through the world not through our bodies but through screens . . .

text: Here, we are meant to feel the effort. To know yourself is to know your limits, and so push your body to the edge of failure.

text: Because of concentration of jobs in high-priced metro areas, effective cost-of-living for people pursuing these jobs has increased even though real cost-of-living (ie for a given good in a given location) hasn’t.

text: Living a constantly balanced life aims to keep all areas of our life at a steady happy medium – but there’s so much beauty and life in letting ourselves get lost in one area or the other from time to time. Living life in seasons recognizes and embraces that. It’s great to have some seasons that are more imbalanced than others – giving yourself a life well lived means allowing yourself to indulge in whatever your heart desires from time to time.
author: Erifili

text: What if I told you this hunger to endure everything, this ceaseless reaching, this need to feel something more, is not curiosity, but self-exile? . . . But you were only ever meant to come home to yourself. To your own food; to your own bed.
author: Amber (Ode to a Poet Substack)

text: People often build artificial heavens around the goals they chase and artificial hells around the anxieties they run away from. This framing can fuel short bursts of motivation, but it is an unsustainable way to live for any length of time. Scarcity and anxiety distort decision making and leaves you prone to ideological capture.
author: Alex (Scimitar Capital)

text: The key to living a productive life is always to minimize: You want to have as few things as possible to give yourself enough space.

text: I think it’s that I want to be really deliberate about the imperfect, unfinished nature of my work.
author: Visakan Veerasamy

text: I don’t know if anything is ever really that straightforward, but I’ve definitely been in the wrong part of that cycle within myself- where I hide my disappointment and fear and insecurity from myself, and as a consequence sever my connection with myself, and become something of a disembodied ghost in my own life.
author: Visakan Veerasamy

text: There can be a murkiness between what you think is right, and what actually feels right, and it can be shockingly, troublingly easy for one’s thoughts to smother one’s feelings . . . But it can be difficult to face those feelings to begin with, one of the strongest reasons being that acknowledging these ‘darker’ feelings is itself something that feels risky.
author: Visakan Veerasamy

text: What happens when you are miserable and in comparison mode? You lack the energy and drive. . . . The only comparison you should be doing is you vs. you previous year. . . . There is a good chance that with five years of effort, you could have more than they do.
author: Boss Letter

text: Our advice here is to give in. Don’t be too hard on yourself, especially if you are a young person already working on your mission and goals. You have too much space to be spontaneous and impulsive. As a result, those memories will last a lifetime. Trust us on this . . . You will not regret it.
author: Boss Letter

text: If you want to be where others are not, you have to live in a way no one else does . . . When everyone is eating slop food. You eat clean. When everyone is spending their time watching Netflix. You study. When everyone is getting into debt. You invest in assets.
author: Boss Letter

text: That one time, somewhere later in life, you are finally free to do the things you always wanted to do. Read this last sentence again. It sounds miserable. Because it is miserable. The entire concept of retirement has been misunderstood and will continue to be. Retirement is a state of mind.
author: Boss Letter

text: Everyone knows someone who goes to the gym, does only a few compound movements, and eats the right food. That same person often beats those who half-ass their 6-day splits, not taking nutrition seriously, and taking a bunch of supplements. . . . It is always about minimizing and focusing on the things that actually matter.
author: Boss Letter

text: Replace podcasts, audiobooks, and music with phone calls: Next time you are driving or walking somewhere where you need to be . . . The time you have would be better spent by calling and talking to the people you care about. It is the #1 way to show people you appreciate them and to keep them in your life.
author: Boss Letter

text: You are just one DM (or email) away from changing your life: . . . Start contacting the people you admire, those who inspire you, and those who can give you the opportunities you want to be a part of. . . . It is one of those things that has no negative consequences, yet the positives are hard to match.
author: Boss Letter

text: Never tell anyone how much money you make: . . . There is no reason you should tell anyone how well you are doing. . . . It is a net negative game that only brings enemies.
author: Boss Letter

text: Someday you would give anything for just 3 minutes of this: Mindset one. Big one. Powerful one. Baby crying at 2am? Partner complaining about their day? Parents pissing you off with their old-world takes? All of us will find ourselves in a position where we think the same thought.
author: Boss Letter

text: One trait that’s in common with all high agency people I’ve met: they have humility. Their ego doesn’t run their life. They’re not afraid to ask for help. And they can be wrong and not break down crying like my 2 year old toddler.
author: Tim Denning

text: Here’s the cold-ass truth. Not diversifying is incinerating money. Looking back at your concentrated outcome and saying “see” is not proof of anything but survivorship.
author: Kris Abdelmessih

text: The fastest traders want slower data to be widely available, because it means that they’ll have more counterparties to trade with; a world where retail investors still have 15-minute delayed quotes . . . is a world where the fastest traders will represent more of the total liquidity, and bid/ask spreads will be correspondingly larger.
author: Byrne Hobart

text: What we should care about is our body’s physiological response, and that is what resting physiology captures (the output, not your behavior, which is the input).
author: Marco Altini

text: I don’t know where I heard it, but someone said the reason some finance people stay in finance (unhappily) long past satisfying their financial goals is that they can’t do anything else. Not in a “they lack the ability” but in a learned helplessness kind of way. They cannot stomach the hit to their identity, status, or sense of usefulness, even if all of it is in vain.
author: Kris Abdelmessih

text: But something to remember is that there is always some unknown part of the future that you will be equally fond of. . . . And after every other transition in my life, there were likewise things to love that I couldn’t have previously pictured.
author: Cate Hall

text: Try it. Go around your day, narrating all of your choices to yourself. With everything you do, consciously say, in your head: “I am choosing to do this, because it’s the best course of action according to all the information I have available.” See if it feels true.
author: Cate Hall

text: We are surrounded by grand examples of ambition. Bottomless appetites for wealth and power. But figuring out how to live on your terms, around people you are happy to be around, working on things that light you up, and staying true to your values is an ambitious goal. Pulling that off is hard because unless you got lucky and ended up on YOUR path from the start, at some point you will need to know when to quit.
author: Kris Abdelmessih

text: A productive learning session feels like the cognitive equivalent of an intense physical workout. . . . The satisfaction comes from pulling through and achieving something that you know took real work, something that you really earned. If you don’t go for something that takes real work, something you have to earn, you just waste away in a state of “meh”.
author: Justin Skycak

text: Math academy is one of the few online courses I’ve done that actually makes me think, gets me annoyed when I get things wrong and gives me the feeling progress when I get things right. Almost all other courses all have the same neutral feeling of “meh, next video” or even worse feeling completely bored while the instruction video is playing.
author: @DSDecoded

text: A recurring theme: calibration is everything. Knowing where you are in a pecking order and choosing your actions in light of that is a life skill. You don’t need to be especially smart to do that, but you do need to be self-aware. That means interpreting feedback without your defensive ego scrambling the message.
author: Kris Abdelmessih

text: There seem to be two main social purposes to financial markets, or one purpose looked at from two ends: Financial markets allow people to save and participate in economic growth to meet their future material needs, and they help allocate resources to their most productive uses.
author: Matt Levine

text: We’d do a lot more for each other if we acknowledged this fact. Altruism doesn’t need to feel like pure self-flagellation or pure self-congratulation. A lot of the time, if you’re doing it right, it’ll feel irritating. Not all heroes wear capes—some of them wear an exasperated look of “are you seriously trying to lift that couch by yourselves”.
author: Adam Mastroianni

text: Closeness is annoying because it’s about the surrender of control.
author: Ava (bookbear express)

text: Default Mode: Living in reactive mode, exhausting and discouraging. Deliberation: Starting to wrap your arms around life with some intention. Design: Living with a theory of yourself and your values, allowing for detours but with clear direction.
author: Suzy (via Kris Abdelmessih)

text:
[Delivery vans, consumer cars, etc.:] Mostly local, last-mile delivery. The cost tends to be astronomical, often $15 to $200 per ton-mile. Consumers also pay similar rates shopping at retail stores but internalize the costs by sacrificing time and adding personal vehicle miles.

Last-mile and sorting are the majority of the total logistics costs for parcels and deliveries. Labor costs are much higher because a driver carrying 500 pounds of packages costs about the same as a semi-truck driver carrying 30 tons of freight. Packages are unloaded one by one instead of with forklifts. The percentage of cargo weight to vehicle weight is low compared to semi-trucks. These inefficiencies are why many stores are warehouses where customers can load up and make the most of their trip. And why distribution centers for last-mile delivery are close to customers. The proximity allows semi-trucks to carry as many ton-miles as possible.

text:
According to Ericsson, the key to being great is deliberate practice. The key to deliberate practice is motivation.
Parental and authority approval: Initially kids practice because they are given praise and attention from their parents when they do so, and are reprimanded when they don’t.
Peer approval: At some point the young musicians begin to care less about what their parents think, and more about their relative status among their peers . . . a bigger motivation is that their skills are recognized by other young musicians, their true peers.
Self Actualization: Eventually the best musicians stop caring about their peers and start internalizing the desire to be great. They see themselves as musicians, and they do the hard, uncomfortable work of practicing because ‘that is what a great musician does’.
